analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off California, Oregon, and Washington.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 25 House Democrats, was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and died there without ever receiving a hearing, a vote, or action by the full House.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to make it illegal for the Interior Department to sell any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in federal waters off the Pacific coast of California, Oregon, and Washington. The ban would have been permanent, written into law rather than left to each administration's annual offshore leasing plans. The bill went to the House Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing businesses, and tourism economies in California, Oregon, and Washington would gain protection from oil spills and drilling infrastructure in Pacific waters, since the bill would permanently close those waters to new oil and gas leases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast coastal communities and fisheries

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil or natural gas on the outer Continental Shelf off California, Oregon, or Washington [S2][S3].
The prohibition would be permanent and would override any other provision of the leasing law, so future administrations could not reopen West Coast waters to drilling [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to any offshore reserves off the three West Coast states, and the federal government would forgo potential leasing revenue and domestic production from those areas.

drawbacks.text: Permanently closing an entire region to energy development means giving up potential domestic oil and gas supply and the federal royalties that leasing would generate, which critics of drilling bans typically cite as a cost to energy security and taxpayers [S2][S3].

The bill text offers no exception process at all, so it would lock in the ban regardless of future technology or emergency conditions, which is the trade-off inherent in making a moratorium statutory rather than administrative [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For coastal communities the protection is large and one-sided: a major spill off the Pacific coast would impose costs that no royalty revenue could offset, and the bill's permanent, veto-proof structure is the only way to guarantee it. The main cost is forgone energy production in a region that has seen little new offshore leasing in decades, so the immediate economic loss is modest, but the ban is absolute and irreversible by design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress and never received a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2011, by Rep. John Garamendi along with 24 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources [S1][S5].
Five days later it was referred to the subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was recorded for the remainder of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off, since the waters off California, Oregon, and Washington were never permanently closed to leasing, leaving that decision to whichever administration holds office. Coastal communities remain exposed to the risk the bill aimed to remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests and drilling-ready administrations

for.name: Rep. John Garamendi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban oil and gas leasing off the West Coast.

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 25 total Democratic supporters but no Republican support.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; it was referred to a subcommittee and remained there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only partisan signal in the record is that all 25 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have permanently closed West Coast federal waters to new oil and gas leases, cutting off exploration and production in the region. Its death leaves that access available to the industry under future administrations.

industries.industry: West Coast commercial fishing and coastal tourism
industries.note: A permanent drilling ban would protect fisheries, beaches, and coastal economies from spill risk and drilling infrastructure. Because the bill died, that protection was never enacted.
